summary: Design a set with O(1) average insert, remove and getRandom.
mainInsight: Keep values in a list for O(1) random indexing plus a dict from value to its list index. To remove, swap the element with the last one, update the moved element's index, pop the last, and delete the key.

approaches.name: List only
approaches.summary: Insert by append; remove by list.remove.

approaches.name: Dict only
approaches.summary: Hash set; random choice via list(set).

commonMistakes: Forgetting to update the moved element's index
Returning the wrong boolean for duplicates

promptVariants: Which two structures give O(1) insert, remove and getRandom?
Why is one data structure not enough?
options: A list for indexing and a dict from value to index
A heap for removal and a stack for random choice
A sorted array and a binary search tree
Two hash sets that mirror each other
cards.answer: A list for indexing and a dict from value to index
cards.explanation: The list gives random index access; the dict finds an element's index.

incorrectOptionExplanations.Two hash sets that mirror each other: Hash sets cannot pick a random element in O(1).

promptVariants: Why swap with the last element before popping?
cards.answer: Deleting from the middle of a list is O(n) because of shifting. Instead the element to remove is overwritten by the last element, the dict entry of the moved element is updated to the new index, and the last slot is popped (O(1)). Order does not matter in a set, so this is allowed.
cards.explanation: Handle the case where the removed element is the last one.

promptVariants: Complete the statement: Space complexity (excluding the input): ___
cards.explanation: The list and dictionary store n values.

promptVariants: What goes wrong if you remove the last element without checking whether it is the one being removed?
Which order of operations is safest?
options: A stale dict key can remain; move last into place, update its index, then delete
Nothing; the swap works the same when both indices are equal
The list would become unsorted and getRandom would fail then
The dictionary would raise a KeyError on the very next insert
cards.answer: A stale dict key can remain; move last into place, update its index, then delete
cards.explanation: Delete the key after the index update so a single-element removal still ends consistent.

incorrectOptionExplanations.Nothing; the swap works the same when bo: The stale-key ordering matters when they are equal.
incorrectOptionExplanations.The list would become unsorted and getRa: The list does not need to be sorted.
incorrectOptionExplanations.The dictionary would raise a KeyError on: The first insert has nothing to do with it.
